We have moved towards ‘distributed discovery’, where news is not something people intentionally seek out but something they encounter incidentally while browsing their feeds. By repeatedly surfacing content that aligns with a user’s historical data and pre-existing beliefs, these systems can reduce exposure to diverse perspectives and contribute to ideological polarisation. This environment has also contributed to a global rise in ‘news avoidance’, as audiences feel overwhelmed by toxic or emotionally draining content surfaced by engagement-driven metrics.

In this context, the flow of content is organised based on data that the platform collects from users’ interactions. Although it were the editors and the newsroom that decided what and when to show, present and offer, the order of content in the audience’s end, consumed through social media feeds, is now determined by algorithms.

McCombs and Shaw in the Agenda Setting Theory (1972) argue that throughout the history of journalism, it has been up to the editors and newspapers to decide what their audience sees, reads, hears and consequently forms opinions. However, with the advent of digital technology, algorithms influence editorial decisions and control news visibility. Once news gets into social media and other platforms, algorithms dictate what is going to be seen, placed first, recommended, or hidden based on the preferences and interests of each user, not just the news organisations’ criteria.

Algorithms have given rise to what scholars call ‘traffic media’, a business model that aims to maximise and control user attention through algorithmic technologies and corporate policies. At the same time, traditional business models based on advertising and subscriptions have weakened, while technology giants such as Google and Meta have captured a larger share of the digital advertising market. It is important to note that there is growing confrontation over revenue sharing between digital platforms and media organisations. A 2025 study by Peter Chiridza and Admire Mare, titled Digital Platforms and Revenue Generation Strategies Adopted by Zimbabwean Mainstream News Publishers, highlights that most social media platforms do not offer meaningful revenue-sharing partnerships to news publishers, exacerbating these organizations’ economic vulnerabilities.

Early signs of all the shifts described above have gradually emerged in Nepali media ecosystem as well. Some Nepali newsrooms are prioritising news stories based on the degree of audience engagement calculated in terms of clicks, views, shares, likes and other metrics. This has led to an increase in space allotted to lighter genres, such as entertainment, lifestyle, celebrity and highly-shareable content, while neglecting more serious, investigative or public-service journalism. Likewise, journalists in Nepali media are also engaging more directly with social media, including the reporting or re-packaging of issues that have already gone viral. Similarly, at the level of dissemination, newsrooms are increasingly struggling to achieve reach and visibility, as stories that are algorithmically identified, ranked or recommended are more likely to circulate widely.

The way forward is not to resist algorithms but to use them responsibly while preserving journalism’s core values of accuracy, independence, fairness and public interest. In the very spirit, Nepali news organisations should invest in AI and digital literacy so that journalists understand how algorithms shape news visibility and audience engagement. Newsrooms should adopt hybrid models where AI supports tasks such as content discovery, translation, transcription and audience analytics, while journalists retain the editorial decisions.

Nepal can also learn from international practices. The European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA) has introduced stronger platform accountability by requiring transparency about algorithms and measures to address the spread of misinformation. Australia’s News Media Bargaining Code provides an important example of how governments can reduce the unequal bargaining power between digital platforms and news publishers by requiring technology companies to compensate media organisations for news content. Similarly, Nepali media can adopt transparency initiatives inspired by global efforts such as The Trust Project, NewsGuard and the Journalism Trust Initiative, to learn how to promote greater openness about editorial standards, ownership, funding and sources to strengthen public trust.

articles.title: Monsoon disasters demand more than rescue
articles.summary:
Nepal’s monsoon disasters are becoming a grim annual occurrence. Over the past four months, more than 80 people have died in monsoon-related disasters; nine are missing, and 196 have been injured. On Saturday, three people lost their lives in separate landslides in Jajarkot and Rolpa districts, and last week, a mudslide buried a settlement in Rolpa, leaving 10 dead and three missing. Unfortunately, as we are only halfway through the monsoon season, there is a high risk that the death toll will continue to mount. This alarming situation warrants greater seriousness from the government.

Successive governments have consistently failed to prevent the high number of deaths and destruction caused by the monsoon-related disasters. Their aversion to preventing haphazard road construction in different parts of the country has only increased the vulnerability of Nepal’s precarious hill landscape. In many rural hill districts, roads are still built without proper surveys. Local authorities, to meet targets and avoid a budget freeze, often resort to asare bikas, without regard for the dangers of landslides, deaths and displacement. Once constructed, roads are left without proper maintenance and upgrades.

The absence of guidelines about where people can safely build houses in remote hilly areas has also put many lives at risk. At the same time, unregulated riverbed and hill mining has intensified the impact of monsoon-related disasters. For example, in 2024, the Roshi river flood in Kavrepalanchok district killed 78 people, partly due to illegal mining and unregulated crusher industries. Often, these activities occur because of political backing and contract manipulation, yet they operate freely.

In April, Home Minister Sudan Gurung ordered the immediate shutdown of illegal crusher plants after visiting a flood-affected area in Kavrepalanchok district. The Balendra Shah-led government also decided to manage the resources needed to prevent and respond to monsoon-related disasters. Following monsoon disasters, hundreds of rescuers have also been deployed in the affected areas. These steps are welcome but far from enough. Nepal cannot stop the monsoon, nor can it prevent every landslide and flood. But it can mitigate the human costs of predictable disasters.

Shifting the focus from how quickly rescuers reach disaster-affected areas to whether people receive early warnings and whether they trust and act on them is necessary. Equally vital is holding people accountable for haphazard road construction and illegal mining. The public, too, must follow disaster-related early warnings and avoid building homes in risky zones. In Rolpa alone, over 100 households need immediate relocation. Local governments must immediately transfer such vulnerable settlements to safe places and coordinate with the provincial and federal government if necessary. Urgent action is also needed in 134 settlements across all nine local units of Bajura district. In Jajarkot, 200 people who were at risk have been relocated, which is a much-needed step.

The government aimed for zero deaths in monsoon-related disasters this year. Instead, authorities have recorded 85 deaths so far. These deaths must only push the government to acknowledge the fact that it fell short in adequately focusing on prevention before disasters struck. Rather than treating monsoon-related destruction and deaths as an annual ritual like past governments did, it should treat them as a year-round governance challenge and prioritise prevention, early action and preparedness. The government must identify where the risks lie before more disasters and deaths expose them.

articles.title: Mental wellbeing: When a parent goes abroad for work, children can feel a loss that has no end
articles.summary:
When a parent migrates for work, they leave behind fragments of their presence, which, for a child, are never quite enough to make up a whole person.

As parents’ migration for work becomes more normalised in Nepali society, we might be underestimating its psychological cost, a complex understanding of presence and absence in the children’s minds.

Through FaceTime, voice memos, pictures, and videos, their parent’s embrace is known but never truly felt. As a result, they neither become fully connected nor entirely foreign, leading to a sense of ambiguity in their grief.

Sunika Joshi is a mental health professional specialising in trauma, neurodiversity, child and adolescent mental health, and suicide prevention. She is also the co-founder of Lighthouse Neural, a mental health organisation.

Here, she discusses the psychological impact of parental migration on children, how prolonged separation can shape attachment and relationships, and what families can do to protect children’s emotional well-being.

When one parent goes abroad for work, what happens inside a child’s mind in the first few months before the ‘new normal’ sets in?

The new normal depends on who is the caretaker, living arrangements, and sense of security/ safety where they live. Usually, children gradually adapt to new family dynamics.

Initially, children may experience grief-like responses such as sadness, confusion, anger, and somatic complaints like headaches, stomach pain, and sleep issues.

Younger children may show stress in the form of bedwetting, anger issues, and crying over minor issues that are not related to the absence. Adolescents may experience increased worry due to uncertainty, loneliness, and fear.

It can be termed as ambiguous loss, which is a profound sense of loss and sadness that is not death-related; the parent is physically absent but psychologically or emotionally present in some way.

But at the same time, adolescents can also feel a sense of pride if they see it as a sacrifice for the family’s financial security and remain hopeful that their lives will improve—economically and socially.

If the child is young, has the family member explained what migration is and how the living arrangement will change? Is anyone helping the child to make sense of the change? Does the child have access to communicate with the parent who migrated? Questions, as such, matter equally.

There could be many underlying vulnerabilities. If the child has the right support, they can feel hopeful about the future, but if the child is exposed to uncertainty due to debt or illegal ways to go abroad, the risk of being cheated and the family being stressed, the child can also sense the stress and show emotional and behavioral symptoms.

How does prolonged physical absence affect a child’s attachment style? Are these kids more anxious, more avoidant, or does it vary?

What happens during the absence of the parent determines the attachment style. They can be anxious and avoidant. Prolonged separation can increase the risk of both.

Anxious attachment means becoming hypervigilant, fearing abandonment, and worrying about parents’ return, safety, and relationship. Experience emotional vulnerability and loneliness. This attachment happens when caregivers are unable to consistently meet or respond to the young child’s emotional and physical needs. Later in life, they might struggle with anxiety in relationships, making them ‘clingy’ or jealous.

Avoidant attachment means to learn to suppress and avoid emotional conversations, spending time with family, or communicating their issues. Children may become self-reliant and push people away; don’t actively seek out their caregiver for comfort or emotional support. It results when a young child loses a sense of security in their environment. It can lead to suspicion, hostility, and lack of commitment in later relationships.

But these depend on the child’s temperament, the consistency of the substitute caregiver and how communication with the absent parent is handled.

But when caregiving is inconsistent, children are likely to show anxiety, depressive symptoms, and challenges in forming an emotional bond with friends and family.

Can a strong emotional bond survive almost entirely through video calls and voice notes? What gets lost that even daily calls can't replace?

No, physical presence is different than talking on a call. You see the nuances. It is like reading a summary of the book without reading the entire book.

Video calls and voice notes help maintain a sense of connection and can reduce separation anxiety compared to no contact, but cannot fully replace physical presence, especially for younger children.

The child is deprived of physical affection, which is crucial for co-regulation, feeling safe and secure, and forming an attachment to the parent. The child and parent also miss out on the minor, firsthand details of daily routines and what each other's days look like.

Non-verbal communication is largely missing, creating a gap in understanding underlying emotions and in developing attachment through non-verbal cues. And if certain things are not communicated through words or messages, they will be missed.

In the Nepali context, emotional bonds are formed by providing material support in the form of favourite food and gifts. Families do not communicate through words and talk about emotions. In Nepal, fathers, in particular, do not share vulnerability or emotions.

So, this can create a huge gap in building a strong emotional bond as a family. Families would only know about each other through events shared across the device. What gets lost is the bond, trust, and reliability you create through physical presence, making memories by being in the same space and engaging in activities like cooking and celebrating festivals together. Also, passing down the culture, values, knowledge, and the roots of the family/ethnicity/indigeneity.

Is there any age range where a parent’s absence particularly leaves lasting damage?

Yes, in young age and in adolescence.

Younger children, when they have not made sense of the separation and do not understand the change, can show withdrawal and aggression. Early childhood is the time when they learn and understand attachment, love, care, affection, and emotion regulation from their parents, and disruptions in this process can have emotional consequences. Adolescents also face an increasing risk of confusion, loneliness, worry, and uncertainty.

As humans, we are all resilient and can adjust to change, but how a child makes sense of a parent's absence largely depends on the caretaker and guardian, as well as the family's response, the community the child lives in, and the environment.

The connection with the parent can become superficial and may lead to issues with socio-emotional adjustment. A sense of security and trust can also change as the child grows. Psychological well-being declines if more socio-economic challenges arise after migration.

What’s one piece of practical advice you’d give the parent staying behind to protect a child’s emotional development?

Choose a safe and secure place to live and a caregiver. Assess the risk of abuse, assault, discrimination, and neglect from the people around.

Do not pressure the child to take responsibility for the missing parent.

Make sure they understand why the parent migrated; do not expose them to the news of death, accidents, injury, parent separation.

Create space for the child to express their feelings, be vulnerable and if they are showing emotional distress, understand that it can be a reaction to worry and distress.

Do not shut the children and ask them to understand everything.

Help the child to foster a bond with the migrant parent- help them maintain a healthy relationship and communicate.

Avoid putting the child in the middle of adult conflicts about money or return plans.

Seek help from schools, communicate about the change in a child's life.

How does a child’s sense of self develop when one parent exists through a device or a photo rather than a physical presence?

A risk of getting detached from their culture and community surrounds them.

If they are living with relatives, they do not feel a sense of belonging to a family or community. The child will also find it difficult to navigate their emotions toward the parents; they may appreciate the sacrifice and see them as a hero or savior, or they may see them as not being part of the family's struggles and challenges in person.

There might be too much pressure on them to study well, to live with whatever is provided, and not ask for more.

Children also feel pressure to appreciate and repay the sacrifices their parents have made for their future by being overly pressured to excel academically, be smart, and be very ambitious.

This might not provide the child with an area to explore their authentic self, experiment with hobbies and strengths, and make room for any mistake or failure. So living in constant fear and worry and living up to the family’s expectations.

A sense of safety can be hampered.

If the children are taking the role of caretaker and replacing the parent who migrated, girls tend to start taking care of siblings, cooking and cleaning- all household chores. Sons might feel the responsibility for the family’s safety and security. There may be a mutual understanding of sharing struggles and burdens.

Is there a psychological difference between a parent who is dead, divorced, or absent due to migration?

Yes, migration is a different kind of grief. It is an ambiguous loss. The parent is alive and connected through video calls or messages but not present physically. It comes with uncertainty about when they will return, whether they are ever coming back, and also fear of separation from parents, breaking the family apart, and the uncertainty can prolong distress.

Children can also live in emotional conflict- they can feel guilty for being angry at the parent who sacrificed for the family and confused about what to feel.

Death is an irreversible loss and also a socially recognised loss followed by rituals according to the religion they follow. Grieving is mostly getting to terms with the fact that it is permanent and making sense of the loss- physically and emotionally.

Divorce is often breaking off the family dynamics; even if parents are present physically, it also comes with arrangements of who the child lives with and coming to terms with living separately, but both parents are alive.

Do these children struggle more with trust and intimacy later in life, in friendships or romantic relationships?

Trust and intimacy in later life—yes, it can create difficulty in forming strong relationships, trust and feeling secure.

Lower emotional closeness and less contact with parents and family. Causes difficulty trusting others and forming intimate relationships in adulthood. It can also show up in the form of fear of abandonment, getting into unhealthy relationships, and risk of addiction, and not understanding how relationships should be.

Either giving too much or giving too little. Can get into abusive relationships and not be able to recognise it or get out of it. Not understanding the emotional needs of a partner, as well as feeling like not being understood.

articles.title: Nepalis around the world step in to cover footballer Aashish Rai’s medical bills
articles.summary:
It took footballer Aashish Rai over a year of silent suffering to finally speak out. His injury was mishandled from the outset; he was mistreated during rehabilitation; and the All Nepal Football Association, the country’s football governing body, had provided only erratic support.

Even that meagre backing came to a complete halt following FIFA’s suspension of ANFA on June 24. Rai then found himself stranded in Bangkok, Thailand, where the governing body had sent him for treatment. Left with no choice, Rai was forced to go public with his ordeal. He hoped the new Balendra Shah administration would step in to take responsibility for his recovery as he was injured while playing for the country.

But more than a month after the Post reported his ordeal on July 14, state assistance has proven negligible. To date, the government has provided just Rs150,000, through the National Sports Council.

That, however, is nowhere near enough, Rai told the Post over a phone call on Monday. It costs him between Rs450,000 and Rs500,000 per month to cover his treatment, rehabilitation, medication, and stay in Bangkok. “What should I make of Rs150,000?” he said.

Rai had initially held high hopes for the new government, recalling how happy he felt listening to Balendra Shah’s speech on supporting football from the grassroots during his election campaign. Today, however, that optimism has given way to deep disillusionment.

“The issue has also been raised in the parliament,” Rai said. “But the state is yet to respond properly.”

Harka Sampang, chairman of the Shram Sanskriti Party who got elected to the House of Representatives from Sunsari-1, the neighbouring constituency to Rai’s home in Itahari, had raised Rai’s situation in the parliament a week ago.

It is not that the government has not reached out to Rai yet. Apart from the Rs150,000 support through the NSC, Rai got a phone call from a government representative.

“I do not know which ministry or department the person represented,” Rai said. “He said that the government did not have any law to send money abroad.”

For a lack of adequate government support, Nepalis from around the world have stepped in to help Rai, raising funds for him. And this is how Rai is affording his treatment and stay in Bangkok. This constrast between overwhelming public generosity and state indifference highlights a grim reality for Nepali athletes—celebrated when representing the nation, but forced to depend on public charity when injured in its service.

Contributions have poured in for Rai from across the world—from Nepal to Japan to Australia. Nepal United FC in Australia, for instance, has donated him Rs81,000. The Malaysia-based N Penang FC, in coordination with Himalayan FC and Nepbourne FC, collected Rs1.2 million. Shantinagar FC, a club from Rai’s hometown, is also aiming to collect more funds through the 5th Monsoon Football Tournament, which is taking place soon at Budha Subba Football Ground in Itahari. In Japan, Spice Purbeli FC announced that a portion of the proceeds from its upcoming SMILES GOLD CUP 2026 futsal tournament—scheduled for August 30 in Chiba—will be donated to support Rai’s ongoing treatment.

Support has also come in from individual well-wishers, including Prasamsha Bhandari, a ninth-grader at Tender Feet Boarding School in Sundarharaincha, Morang, who donated her Rs1,000 competition prize money to Rai’s cause.

Funds are also being raised through GoFundMe, a crowdfunding platform.

“The way Nepalis around the world supported me with as much money as they could is how I was able to resume my rehabilitation in Bangkok,” Rai said. “I cannot thank them enough.”

Rai was also heartened by a youth rally organised by his friends and supporters in Itahari on Saturday to press the government for immediate intervention. Demonstrators marched holding placards reading, “Applause when playing for the nation, neglect when injured—how long will this injustice continue?” and “The government must take full responsibility for the treatment and compensation of injured players.”

Public solidarity is there but Rai stresses that meaningful state intervention remains absent.

“The most crucial support—from the state—is still missing,” Rai said. “If given the opportunity, I would like to speak directly with Education and Sports Minister Sasmit Pokharel to explain my reality.”

When contacted, the NSC stated that it plans to release an additional Rs100,000 for Rai through the Athlete Welfare Fund, bringing its total assistance to Rs250,000.

“We initially dispatched Rs150,000 from an emergency fund designated for accidents involving players or staff—a fund that had a total budget of only Rs700,000,” explained Khush Raj Dahal, spokesperson for the NSC. “We are now arranging to reimburse another Rs100,000 through the Athlete Welfare Fund.”

Asked if Rs250,000 was the maximum state support available to a national athlete injured in service of the country, Dahal cited rigid budgetary constraints.

“We cannot spend funds outside designated budget line items,” Dahal said. “This Rs250,000 is the absolute maximum we can extend under current rules.”

To date, Rai has received just over Rs2 million—including the NSC’s initial Rs150,000—through donations from well-wishers and crowdfunding efforts worldwide.

Doctors have advised the defender that he will require at least six more months of intensive rehabilitation before he can return home for surgery to remove the hardware in his leg.

“When I last consulted the doctors, they told me I need about six more months of rehab. Only after that can I return to Nepal to remove the steel in my leg,” Rai told the Post. “I have only one fear left: will my treatment come to a halt once again in the coming months for lack of money?”

ANFA has said it would bear all expenses related to Rai’s treatment until he fully recovers and will resume the pending payments and treatment process as soon as the legal and administrative issues surrounding its suspension are resolved. However, given the government’s present handling of the crisis, an immediate resolution—and the lifting of the ban—remains a distant prospect.

Even the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party’s chief whip Prakash Chandra Pariyar raised Rai’s issue at the parliament on Monday. Whether the government will hear the plea of its own party’s member remains to be seen.

articles.title: Thapa faction presses ahead with Congress convention despite Deuba camp’s legal challenge
articles.summary:
The Nepali Congress establishment faction led by party president Gagan Thapa has decided to proceed with the party’s 15th General Convention on October 2-5, rejecting the rival Sher Bahadur Deuba faction’s demand to suspend the process pending a Supreme Court review.

The Central Working Committee concluded its meeting on Monday after discussing the convention schedule and the party’s legal status following the apex court’s decision to review an earlier ruling that had validated Thapa’s presidency. The formal decision on the convention schedule will be announced on Tuesday.

Thapa said the party was constitutionally and legally bound to proceed with the convention.

“The convention will be held in October. There is no question of delaying it,” Thapa told reporters. “The process starts tomorrow, and we want every ward to take part. If anyone responsible for organising the process tries to obstruct it, we will assign the responsibility to someone else. The convention will not stop.”

The Deuba faction, however, says the convention process should remain suspended until the Supreme Court settles the legal dispute over the party’s leadership.

The Supreme Court on August 6 ordered a review of its earlier decision validating the Special General Convention and Thapa’s leadership, giving the Deuba faction new leverage in its challenge to the current party structure.

Congress leader NP Saud said the party should not take decisions with potentially far-reaching consequences while the court is reconsidering the earlier ruling.

“The review means the dispute is still before the court, so the party should not take steps that could fundamentally alter the situation,” Saud said. “If the establishment faction proceeds unilaterally, we will seek an interim order from the court.”

Thapa rejected the argument that the Supreme Court’s review order prevents the party from proceeding with its internal affairs.

“The court will deal with the legal questions, while the party must deal with its organisational affairs,” Thapa said. “The review will determine whether the earlier judgment was consistent with the constitution and the law. It does not mean the court will decide how the party should conduct its internal politics.”

The dispute has deepened a split that has been building since the party’s Special General Convention in January and has now widened into a contest over who has the authority to convene the next regular convention.

The Deuba faction, which met at Chundevi, has declared that the 15th General Convention must be organised by the 14th Central Working Committee under Deuba’s leadership. It has rejected the Special General Convention and the Central Working Committee elected by it as unconstitutional.

But the faction itself is divided over how far it should go in challenging Thapa’s leadership.

Senior leader Shashank Koirala, who led the Chundevi gathering, has called for dialogue between Deuba and Thapa and indicated that he is prepared to recognise Thapa as party president.

“I urged President Gagan Thapa to stay in the leadership and bring everyone together,” Koirala told reporters on Monday. “If that is not possible, we need to find another way forward. Our gathering was about unity, not personal differences. The leadership should sit down and resolve the dispute through dialogue.”

Koirala’s position differs from the formal resolutions adopted by the Deuba faction, which recognise Deuba as the party president and reject Thapa’s leadership. The faction has also placed Deuba’s nameplate at its party contact office.

The disagreement over leadership has been accompanied by differences over the party’s position on religion.

The Deuba faction was unable to release the final document from its Chundevi gathering on Sunday after leaders failed to agree on a provision concerning religion, according to Min Bishwakarma.

“Most issues were agreed upon, but we could not reach a common position on religion,” Bishwakarma said. “Because there was no consensus, we had to postpone the press conference where we were supposed to release the final document.”

The gathering had initially agreed on 19 of 20 proposed points. Disagreement centred on a provision on religion. A subsequent five-point proposal reflected Deuba’s preference for promoting Sanatan religion as a national identity and seeking changes to the constitutional provision on secularism.

Senior leaders including Krishna Prasad Sitaula, Bimalendra Nidhi, Prakash Man Singh and Bishwakarma opposed the revised proposal, preventing the faction from reaching consensus.

The internal differences have complicated the Deuba faction’s attempt to present a united challenge to Thapa’s leadership.

The establishment faction had kept its Central Working Committee meeting running since August 9 while waiting to see how the Deuba faction would position itself after the Chundevi gathering.

Thapa said the party had already moved ahead through decisions taken by the Special General Convention, subsequent parliamentary processes and updates to the party’s legal and organisational framework.

He also criticised Deuba for returning to active party politics after stepping down from the leadership on October 14, 2025, saying his former allies were now drawing him back into an internal power struggle.

“The Central Working Committee gave you a respectful farewell, and we were proud of your contribution,” Thapa said, addressing Deuba. “But some people came back and told you that previous positions would be restored or that you should still be treated as president. Before you returned, none of them had raised these issues.”

Thapa said Deuba would be given due respect as a former party president during the 15th General Convention, but rejected the political significance of the Chundevi resolutions.

“Party policy is decided by the Mahasamiti, General Convention or Special General Convention,” he said. “Decisions taken at an informal gathering cannot change the party’s constitution or official policy.”

General secretary Pradeep Paudel also criticised Deuba for aligning himself with the faction rather than helping resolve the dispute.

“We expected the former president to return as a referee, but he came back wearing the jersey of one side,” Paudel said. “That has made reconciliation more difficult. Instead of weakening the party, he should come to the party office at Sanepa, help strengthen it and take part in shaping its policies.”

articles.title: The trouble with sexuality education in Nepal is too much of it goes untaught
articles.summary:
The girl had only asked a question.

Seema (name changed) was in grade 7 in Rithapata in Bhajang District, when her teacher first explained that human reproduction involved intercourse, embryos and how bodies work. She went home and asked her parents about it. Her father slapped her. Then he walked to the school and told the teachers they were teaching his daughter unnecessary things.

Sauriya Budhathoki, 17, a student at Divya High School in Kathmandu, had a different experience. She says she was lucky because of one teacher. A female English teacher at her school took it upon herself to go beyond the curriculum. “She told us that in her time, they weren’t taught these things so she wanted us to learn about it early,” Sauriya said. But the subject disappeared the following year. There was no Health, Population and Environment (HPE) in grade 9.

What the school didn’t teach her, her older sister did — partially. What she wishes had come earlier, and from school, is simple: “Periods and bodily changes, should have been explained to us much earlier, rather from grade 5 or 6.”

Two students, two different locations and entirely different education about their own bodies. The difference was not policy but luck: the particular teacher, the particular school and the particular year.

Seven years ago, Nepal’s education officials made a series of public commitments on Comprehensive Sexuality Education (CSE). Lekha Nath Poudel, then director general of the Curriculum Development Centre, said CSE would be introduced in phases from grade 1, while the Ministry of Education said a mandatory policy was forthcoming. At the time, international organisations including UNESCO, UNFPA and UN Women were also running a pilot programme in Bajura, Achham, Sunsari, Rautahat and Sarlahi districts.

Seven years later, the gap between those commitments and what students experience in classrooms remains wide. CSE content is incorporated into the curriculum through grade 8, but much of it appears only in one or two chapters and remains limited in scope, leaving students with only surface level understanding.

At grades 9 and 10, when adolescents are navigating puberty, relationships, Health, Physical Education remains an optional subject. Teachers and experts say CSE remains limited and heavily dependent on support from international organisations, while lessons are often skipped in classrooms.

The curriculum does cover these topics, on paper. For grades 1 to 3, age-appropriate topics like good touch and bad touch, family and personal hygiene are included in Hamro Serofero, the interdisciplinary subject that covers surroundings, social studies, and science. From grade 4, CSE is incorporated into Health, Physical Education and Creative Arts as a compulsory subject, with three credit hours per week. “Grade 6 has a dedicated unit on Sexual and Reproductive Health,” said Kamal Prasad Mishra, a curriculum officer at the CDC. “Grade 7 introduced LGBTQI+ content. Grade 8 covers puberty, menstruation and nocturnal emissions.”

At grades 9 and 10, where four credit hours are allocated, the subject becomes optional.

“The content exists just in definitions and delivery remains surface-level, a topic here and there, rarely enough to give students a real framework,”said Meena Sharma, chairperson of Institute of Human Rights Communication Nepal (IHRICON), a human rights organisation.

The decision to make Health optional at the secondary level was made by the National Curriculum Development and Evaluation Council, chaired by then federal education minister, partly because students were considered overloaded. The practical consequences play out not in policy documents but in staffing rosters. Because the subject is not compulsory, many schools have no dedicated teaching position for it.

Prabin Khadka, youth and CSE manager at the Family Planning Association of Nepal, said teachers of subjects such as mathematics or English are often asked to teach CSE despite lacking the necessary competence.

At Manakamana Secondary School in Harion, Sarlahi, Mina Dhungana Baral, a Social Studies teacher teaches HPE in grade 8 despite it not being her area of expertise. She has received no formal CSE training. “I think Science teachers would be better equipped to teach the technical details of reproductive health and gender identity than I am,” she said.

She has nevertheless found ways to teach the subject. Students are curious but often hesitant to ask questions. She said teachers have to find or create their own materials and need formal training on how to approach sensitive topics.

Her principal, NT Lama, said the school had received neither adequate materials nor training from the government. He has noticed students becoming visibly uncomfortable when lessons on consent or reproductive health come up.

“If we had been teaching them this content from a young age, they would not be reacting that way,” he said.

It is a problem the government says it is working to fix. Ram Chandra Dhakal of the Centre for Education and Human Resource Development (CEHRD), said his office runs a one-month certification programme for HPE teachers in grades 4 to 8 and a customised five-day programme. Ministry of Education spokesperson Shree Prasad Bhattarai said 1,500 teachers are benefiting from the latter.

A more targeted intervention came this year in the form of a Training of Trainers conducted in collaboration with FPAN and supported by UNFPA through KOICA, the Korean aid agency. Dhakal said CEHRD coordinated with Education Training Centres across all seven provinces to invite participants. Of the twenty-five teachers invited, 24 teachers came from across the country, which has around 26,000 community schools. And the training is not held annually, because it depends on funding.

What happens after teachers return to their classrooms is also unclear. Dhakal said monitoring falls to local governments. Mishra said the CDC is primarily occupied with curriculum development and lacks the resources for consistent field feedback.

The reasons teachers skip CSE lessons are not difficult to find. Khadka said hesitation is one of the most persistent barriers.

“Local teachers often find it difficult to teach these topics as students who are their relatives or neighbours are in the same class,” he said.

In provinces like Sudurpaschim, superstitions around menstruation make the subject harder still. Parents, he said, often believe CSE is only about sexual relationships and fear it will lead children towards “immoral behaviour”. “In reality, CSE covers gender-based violence prevention, communication skills and life skills.”

A 2025 Nepali study on CSE delivery in schools found the same pattern. Teachers often focused on abstinence rather than factual information. Students were left with questions because teachers were too uncomfortable to discuss the topic openly. Its title captured what students themselves reported: “The teacher himself feels shy, so how can we ask questions to him?”

Sharma, who has conducted fieldwork across Karnali, Madhesh and Sudurpaschim provinces, described what that hesitation looks like from the other side of the classroom. In Madhesh, she said, teachers often laugh the subject off. In Baitadi, she documented a case where a mathematics teacher would reach into female students’ pockets under the pretext of looking for chocolates or erasers. The students said nothing. They were weak in mathematics and afraid. “There was no complaint mechanism,” she said. “At the same time, they had no word for what actually happened to them. They were not aware of the concept of good touch or bad touch and consent.”

The consequences of that gap show up in the data. A recent report by the Centre for Research on Environment Health and Population Activities found that even as Nepal reduced adolescent pregnancy nationally, from 56 percent to 14 percent between 2001 and 2022, Madhesh and Karnali recorded the highest rates throughout the entire period. They are the same provinces where Sharma says CSE delivery is weakest.

The classrooms themselves compound the problem. In regions like Karnali and Sudurpaschim, significant age gaps exist within a single grade, a 13-year-old sitting beside an 18-year-old who has returned from working in India. Their needs, their exposure and their understanding of what CSE content means are entirely different. “Schools must create safe spaces,” Sharma said. “But they are not equipped to.”

With internet penetration in Nepal now above 80 percent, students are not waiting for the next class to find answers. “Curious minds need more than just lectures,” she said. “They need audio-visual methods to be impactful. Students often have half-knowledge and explore other options because HPE classes aren’t as regular as Math or Science.”

For many students, there is nowhere to turn when something goes wrong. According to Nepal Police data, an average of seven to eight rape cases are reported every day in the country, roughly 2,200 to 2,300 cases annually. In the fiscal year 2017-18, 64 percent of rape victims were girls below age 18. It was partly in response to this that Nepal Police launched the Community- Police Partnership programme in 2018. Abi Narayan Kafle, spokesperson for Nepal Police, confirmed the programme is still ongoing, with Police-School Liaison Committees established across the country. Through it, officers visit schools to teach students about sexual harassment, good touch and bad touch, and rape prevention. But the programme operates under the Ministry of Home Affairs, not the Ministry of Education and a police awareness programme, however well-intentioned, is not a substitute for a compulsory curriculum.

Mishra at CDC was direct about the limits of what his office can do. “It happens through stakeholder pressure: from students, teachers and society. It is a matter for the Ministry and political leadership.” He added: “I personally feel it would be good if HPE were compulsory for grades 9-10 as well. However, this won’t happen just because I say so.”

Sharma disagreed with that approach. “It is better to invest in health education early than to spend on health services later,” she said. “It should be made mandatory.”

articles.title: Indian army chief conferred honorary general of Nepali Army
articles.summary:
Indian Army Chief General Dhiraj Seth has been conferred the honorary rank of General of the Nepali Army by President Ramchandra Paudel during a ceremony at Sheetal Niwas on Monday.

The event was attended by Vice President Ramsahay Prasad Yadav, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Chief Secretary Govinda Bahadur Karki, and Chief of Army Staff Ashok Raj Sigdel, alongside former army chiefs. Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who currently holds the defence portfolio, was absent. According to sources at the prime minister’s office, General Seth is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Shah on Tuesday.

Official records at Nepali Army Headquarters show that the tradition of conferring the honorary rank of general on each other’s army chiefs began in 1950. However, military historians trace the practice back to the era of Rana Prime Minister Bir Shumsher. Military officials note that this tradition reflects strong military and political ties, though it has been paused during past diplomatic strains, such as the 1989 blockade when planned visits were omitted.

Army Spokesperson Rajaram Basnet highlighted the significance of the tradition, describing it as a reflection of deep-rooted connections. “This unique tradition represents the continuity of cultural, religious, historical, and friendly military relations between Nepal and India,” said Basnet. He added that General Seth paid tribute to brave soldiers at the Army Pavilion in Tundikhel and inspected a guard of honour at Army Headquarters, where he also handed over military and medical supplies provided under military assistance.

Earlier on Monday, General Seth held a courtesy meeting with Chief of Army Staff Sigdel to discuss mutual interests and bilateral military relations. During his three-day visit, General Seth will address trainees at the Army Command and Staff College in Shivapuri, interact with instructors and foreign trainees, and attend a gathering of former Gurkha soldiers in Pokhara before returning home.

articles.title: TB treatment is free in Nepal, but 51 percent of affected families face crippling costs: Report
articles.summary:
Laxmi Chaudhary from Dhangadhi Sub-metropolitan City in Kailali district has been living in Kathmandu for the past one year for treatment of gland TB, medically known as tuberculous lymphadenitis.

The 54-year-old was referred to Bir Hospital by doctors at Seti Provincial Hospital in Dhangadhi after her condition did not improve even after a year of medication.

“In the initial stage, she used to come to Kathmandu every month,” said Dr Prajowl Shrestha, senior chest physician and associate professor at the National Academy of Medical Sciences. “But when she ran out of money, she decided to rent a room in Kathmandu. Expenses were huge, as she had to bring her family members also.”

Although tuberculosis medicines are provided free of charge in Nepal, a new study shows that 51 percent of households with a TB patient face catastrophic costs due to the disease.

According to a report titled ‘Catastrophic Costs and Impoverishment Among Tuberculosis-Affected Households in Nepal: Results from a National Patient Cost Survey,’ free medicines and clinical services alone are not enough to protect TB-affected families from financial hardship.

These costs include spending on medical tests, transportation, food and accommodation, as well income lost due to illness.

“One in two TB-affected households in Nepal face catastrophic costs despite free diagnosis and treatment,” the report published recently in Health Policy and Planning, a peer-reviewed international scientific journal published by Oxford University Press, stated. “Drug-resistant TB leaves three in four affected households facing catastrophic costs in Nepal.”

Tuberculosis, or TB, is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which most commonly affects the lungs. When people with pulmonary TB cough, sneeze, or spit, they release TB bacteria into the air, and people who inhale them can become infected.

Along with medicines, the government provides sputum testing and chest x-rays free of charge for TB diagnosis, but patients must pay out of pocket for other investigations, including CT scans, MRI scans, and some laboratory tests, which can be costly.

“Some TB patients also have to undergo cerebrospinal fluid analysis, tissue biopsies and pleural fluid tests,” said Dr Shrestha, who is a principal investigator of the study. “These and other tests do not come under the free scheme.”

Besides the lungs, TB can affect other parts of the body, including the lymph nodes, bones and joints, brain, kidneys, urinary tract, abdomen, intestines, liver, spleen, reproductive organs, skin and eyes, and multiple tests are required to diagnose the ailments, Shrestha said.

The study, which included 1,000 patients enrolled in the National Tuberculosis Programme, found that the financial burden was primarily driven by direct non-medical costs, which accounted for 44 percent of the total costs.

Direct medical costs included out-of-pocket payments for consultations, laboratory tests, and medications. Direct nonmedical costs comprised expenditures for transportation, food, accommodation, and nutritional supplements or additional food.

Indirect costs, mainly income lost due to illness and treatment, accounted for another 39 percent. Indirect costs represented the economic value of time lost due to illness and care-seeking and were estimated using the human-capital approach.

Total costs for the entire TB episode were estimated by aggregating three components: pretreatment costs, intensive-phase costs, and continuation-phase costs, according to the report.

Of the total participants, over one-third (36 percent) were the primary income earner in their households.

“TB-related costs pushed 13 percent of households below the poverty line, increasing to 31 percent among DR-TB households,” reads the report.

Overall, 35 percent of participants reported borrowing money to cover treatment-related expenses, including 42percent of those with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) and 31 percent of those with drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB).

A smaller proportion had to sell assets such as land, livestock or gold jewellery to meet these expenses—5.7 percent of DS-TB patients and 7.7 percent of DR-TB patients.

Nepal continues to face a substantial TB burden. According to the latest WHO estimates, around 67,000 people developed TB in Nepal in 2024, equivalent to an incidence rate of 227 cases per 100,000 population. TB also caused an estimated 16,000 deaths in the country that year— 44 people every day.

Of the estimated 67,000 people who developed TB in 2024, only 38,606 were diagnosed and received treatment, leaving a substantial number of people with the disease undetected and untreated. Health officials say these missing cases pose a serious challenge to controlling the further spread of TB.

“Finding hidden cases in communities is the main challenge for us in controlling tuberculosis,” said Dr Bhuwan Paudel, director of the National Tuberculosis Control Centre. “Despite various efforts, we have not been able to detect all the estimated TB patients.”

Nepal has committed to ending TB through the WHO End TB Strategy by 2035. But the National Prevalence Survey carried out in 2018-19 with the technical and financial support from the WHO showed that the country is “not on track’ to meet the target.

The survey estimated that 117,000 people were living with TB at the time.

Nepal started providing TB treatment some 93 years ago, but it continues to remain one of the major public health burdens.

Dr Shrestha said Chaudhary needs extended treatment, which could last several months, and he must remain under close supervision by medical personnel.

“I have already spent all I could in my treatment,” Shrestha quoted Chaudhary as complaining. “Now, there is no one in my village to provide additional loans either.”

articles.title: Exhibit review: When an oral story becomes a painting
articles.summary:
Artist Bivas Rai’s solo exhibition ‘Myth & Memory’ will open at Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, on August 28.

Presented by the Australian Himalayan Foundation (AHF) and Siddhartha Art Gallery, the exhibition brings together paintings that explore Kirati Rai culture through Sakela, a communal dance and festival celebrated to honour nature and ancestors.

Rai, recipient of the 2025 AHF Himalayan Art Award, grew up in an extended Rai family surrounded by stories. As a child, however, he says he rarely had the patience to listen to them. Years later, his relationship with those stories has changed.

“Indigenous history is primarily passed down in the form of stories from one generation to the next,” says Rai. His growing curiosity about the stories he once avoided led him to spend the past year observing, listening to, and archiving accounts shared by elders in his family.

Rather than trying to establish a single authoritative version, ‘Myth & Memory’ works within this shifting nature of folklore.

Sakela provides the visual language for the series. Its silli, or dance movements, often imitate elements of nature, including animals and flowers. While Sakela sets the visual tone, Rai says the exhibition is rooted in sisterhood and matriarchy.

Every painting in the series features one of his sisters. Rai connects the women he grew up with to the Kirati myth of Tayama and Khiyama, the primordial sisters, allowing familial memory and inherited mythology to occupy the same space.

“My world has been shaped entirely by the strength and presence of my mother, her sisters, and my own sisters,” says Rai.

Through ‘Myth & Memory’, these recollections are carried from oral storytelling into painting, preserving them while acknowledging that memory itself continues to shift each time a story is retold.

The exhibition will be inaugurated by Australian Ambassador to Nepal Simon Ernst, AHF Chair Garry Weare, and AHF Himalayan Art Award founder Margie Thomas.

Myth & Memory

When: August 28 to September 20Where: Siddhartha Art Gallery, Baber Mahal Revisited, KathmanduOpening: August 28, 5:30 pm

articles.title: Visits reopen talks to rescue bankrupt Gorakhkali Rubber Industry
articles.summary:
Repeated government inspections of the Gorakhkali Rubber Industry have yet to produce a concrete plan to restart the long-shuttered factory.

Another inspection was carried out on Sunday as the government again studies possible models to bring the state-owned plant back into operation.

The factory has been shut since March 2015, and years of neglect have left its machinery, buildings and other infrastructure in deteriorating condition.

Kabindra Burlakoti, the newly elected member of the House of Representatives from Gorkha-2, visited the factory for the third time since the March parliamentary election. A subcommittee under the government’s Public Assets Management Committee led the latest inspection at the factory in Gorkha Municipality-13.

Burlakoti, fellow federal lawmaker Sushil Khadka and officials from the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies inspected the closed factory. Residents urged the team to settle on a clear operating model before moving ahead.

“Everyone would be happy to see the factory reopen, but the government needs to say how it plans to run it,” said Pratap Bhandari of Gorkha Municipality-13. “Will the government operate it, privatise it or hand it over to another institution? That needs to be clear.”

Residents complained that government teams have repeatedly inspected the factory without deciding on how to restart it. Resident Ishwor Pariyar said the plant should resume production using its existing technology and gradually shift to newer technology.

“It would be better to start with the technology already in place and upgrade it over time,” Pariyar said. “If the factory reopens, the younger generation will have jobs and local farmers will have an easier market for even small amounts of vegetables and milk. The local economy will become more active. We just need a decision on how to move forward.”

Khadka, also coordinator of the subcommittee, said the government is studying 38 public enterprises across the country. Gorakhkali Tyre, which was shut down while still operational, has been given priority as the government assesses options for its revival.

“We came for a field inspection because the government needs a report from the ground before deciding on an operating model,” Khadka said. “There is no reason why this factory cannot be brought back into operation. The due diligence assessment also concluded that it can be operated.”

The government is now looking at a more efficient operating model, he said.

“Gorakhkali Tyre is a project of national pride. We grew up hearing about Gorakhkali Tyre, and everyone wants to hear that name again,” Khadka said.

Burlakoti said the factory’s buildings and infrastructure have deteriorated after being left idle for years.

“People ask when it will reopen, but we cannot give a definite date yet,” he said. “Within a few months, however, we expect to settle on a model for its operation.”

He said immediate attention would be given to cleaning and repairing the site. The factory’s machinery and vehicles have been left to deteriorate, while weeds and plants have grown around the buildings.

“The factory was shut while it was still operating, so the vehicles and machinery have been sitting idle and deteriorating. After 10 to 12 years of closure, plants have grown inside the buildings, moss has spread, and windows have broken,” Burlakoti said. “We should start repairs immediately so that the factory is not left in the same condition when the next inspection team arrives.”

Gorakhkali Rubber Industry frequently becomes a political talking point during elections, but repeated government studies and task forces have failed to produce a concrete plan for its revival.

A government task force had previously proposed privatising the factory, citing its low production capacity and outdated technology. The proposal also sparked interest from the private sector. Chinese investors have repeatedly visited the factory to explore the possibility of investing in its revival, but no firm operating plan has emerged.

The factory fell silent after the government introduced a voluntary retirement scheme for its workers and employees in January 2019. It has not returned to operation since.

Years of neglect have taken a toll on the plant. Its machinery has begun to rust and deteriorate, while its buildings and other facilities have fallen into disrepair. The factory has 42 residential blocks that once housed 42 employee families, but the staff quarters are now largely deserted.

The factory occupies 682 ropanis of land (one ropani equals 0.05087 hectares) at Deurali, near the entrance to Gorkha district headquarters. Gorakhkali Rubber Industry began producing tyres on December 14, 1992, becoming the first tyre manufacturer in Nepal.

articles.title: Supreme Court orders release of journalist Kishor Shrestha
articles.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday ordered the release of journalist Kishor Shrestha, directing police to continue their investigation without keeping him in custody.

A division bench of justices Nahakul Subedi and Balkrishna Dhakal issued the order while hearing a habeas corpus petition filed by Shrestha’s wife, Saraswati Shrestha.

Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Prasad Koirala said Shrestha would be investigated while remaining outside custody.

“The writ petition was heard and an order has been issued for his release,” Koirala said. “He will be released after police complete the necessary documentation and legal procedures.”

The bench ordered the Kathmandu District Police Range to investigate Shrestha on a personal bond or bail under Section 15 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 2017.

It found that the circumstances did not warrant keeping Shrestha in custody for the investigation. The order noted that the photograph cited in the complaint had been posted on Facebook by the complainant herself.

The justices also mentioned that although Shrestha is the editor of the weekly Jana Aastha, there was no indication that he held an editorial role at the online portal involved in the complaint.

The order further said complaints concerning news content should be dealt with by the Press Council Nepal, the media sector’s regulatory body. Keeping Shrestha in custody in such circumstances would be contrary to the right to communication guaranteed by Article 19 of the Constitution, it said.

The bench also ordered authorities to return six CPUs and two laptops seized from the Jana Aastha office and Shrestha’s residence. The equipment is to be handed back in the presence of the Supreme Court registrar.

Shrestha, editor of the weekly Jana Aastha, was arrested on August 12 by a joint team from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office and the Kathmandu District Police Range. Police are investigating him on allegations of violating the Privacy Act, 2018.

Earlier on Monday, the Kathmandu District Court had authorised police to keep Shrestha in custody for another four days for investigation after his initial three-day detention period expired.

articles.title: PM Shah to face lawmakers’ questions on August 26
articles.summary:
Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal on Monday set August 26 as the date for Prime Minister Balendra Shah to appear in the House of Representatives and answer questions from lawmakers.

At the start of Monday’s House meeting, Aryal directed Shah to attend the House and respond to lawmakers’ questions under the provisions of the House of Representatives Rules, 2026. At the end of the meeting, he announced the date for the question-and-answer session with the prime minister.

“I inform the House that the direct question-and-answer session with the prime minister, under Chapter 9 of the House of Representatives Rules, 2026, has been scheduled for the meeting on August 26,” Aryal said.

The session will allow at least one lawmaker from each parliamentary party represented in the House to put a question to the prime minister, Aryal said. Up to 15 additional questions will be selected based on the proportional representation of the parties in the House.

Lawmakers wishing to question the prime minister must submit their questions in writing to the secretary of the House by 1 pm on Friday, Aryal said. He also urged lawmakers to keep their questions brief.

The announcement formalises the question-and-answer session that opposition lawmakers have been seeking from Shah over issues under his responsibility.

At the start of Monday’s meeting, Aryal had directed Shah to attend the House and answer lawmakers’ questions, citing provisions in Rules 56 to 60 governing direct questions to the prime minister.

Aryal said he had taken note of lawmakers’ repeated demands for a question-and-answer session on important matters concerning the prime minister and his areas of responsibility.

The directive came amid continuing opposition demands for Shah to explain remarks he made during a House meeting on May 31, when he said Nepal had also encroached on Indian territory.

Opposition lawmakers have since been pressing the prime minister to clarify the remarks. Aryal’s directive on Monday, however, did not specifically refer to the controversy over Shah’s statement.

Chapter 9 of the House rules governs direct question-and-answer sessions with the prime minister. Rule 56 provides for the first hour of one House meeting during the first week of every month to be allocated for lawmakers to ask the prime minister questions on important matters directly related to him or his areas of responsibility.

articles.title: At Re-Kriti, the product is the hero
articles.summary:
Growing up in New Road, one of Kathmandu’s busiest shopping hubs, Nasana Bajracharya watched her neighbourhood change around her.

Stores that once sold food, electronics, and other goods gradually became clothing shops. By the time she finished school, she remembers seeing clothes almost everywhere she looked.

It left her with a question. “Who wears these many clothes?” she wondered. And if people were buying so much, what happened to everything they no longer wore?

During the second year of her BBA, she participated in a startup idea competition. When asked to come up with a business idea, textile upcycling was the first thing that came to her.

That idea eventually became Re-Kriti.

Four years into its work, Re-Kriti has upcycled around 2,200 kilograms of jeans. More than 700 customers have handed over their old jeans to be transformed into bags. The organisation has also provided income-generating opportunities to 11 women artisans.

But getting people to see an old pair of jeans as raw material rather than rubbish has not always been easy.

“People did think that products made from discarded fabric are of low quality,” she says. Some expected products to cost between Rs200 and Rs500 simply because the material had already been used. The reasoning was: If it is old, why should I pay much for it?

For Bajracharya, Nepal’s textile waste problem cannot be separated from the fast-fashion industry. Clothing stores have multiplied, online shopping has expanded, and people are consuming more clothes without necessarily using what they already own.

And getting rid of clothes does not necessarily solve the problem either. Donation is often treated as an easy answer to unwanted clothing. But Re-Kriti’s founder argues that donating transfers the responsibility if there is no demand for what is being given.

Charity and thrift stores can also accumulate clothing that nobody wants, leaving the problem unresolved.

At Re-Kriti, however, clothes that have already reached that point are given another possibility.

Some materials arrive from garment factories, where unused fabric may be discarded despite being new. Others are purchased from thrift stores that have been unable to sell them. Customers also bring in their own old jeans.

Used denim is washed, sorted and eventually cut and stitched into new products. During its early days, the team could use only around 60 to 70 percent of a pair of jeans.

Today, the founder estimates that around 95 percent of each pair can be upcycled. Pockets and smaller pieces can become wallets, key rings and bag charms. She says only a few sections, such as the zipper and upper belt portion, remain difficult to repurpose.

Working with waste, it turns out, requires learning how to waste less of it.

The organisation deliberately works with local women artisans, particularly home-based tailors. Women may receive sewing and other vocational training through municipalities, wards, and different programmes, but learning a skill does not guarantee having somewhere to use it.

Household and caregiving responsibilities can make conventional working hours difficult. And when women cannot commit to a 10-to-6 job, formal employment opportunities shrink.

Re-Kriti therefore designed part of its production around home-based work, sending quality-checked materials to the artisans.

Of the 11 women who have received income opportunities through Re-Kriti, six currently receive consistent work, while five others are engaged when production increases.

She remembers one home-based tailor who had previously been poorly paid and treated badly elsewhere but had few alternatives. After beginning to earn through Re-Kriti, the founder says she noticed a change not only in her income but also in her confidence.

The first two years, Bajracharya says, felt like “hitting a wall”.

People sometimes bought Re-Kriti products because they admired the cause. That support was encouraging, but she quickly realised it was not enough to sustain a business.

So Re-Kriti studied online inquiries, marketplace responses and feedback from previous customers to understand what people actually wanted.

That process led to one of the most important lessons Re-Kriti has learned about sustainability.

“The product is the hero,” the founder says.

In the beginning, Re-Kriti emphasised words like ‘upcycled’ and ‘sustainable’. For people already concerned about the environment, that message could be persuasive.

For everyone else, sustainability alone was not enough; the product also had to be attractive and useful.

That realisation pushed Re-Kriti to invest more in product development, marketing and how its work was presented on social media.

Sometimes, however, the old material carries a value that no new fabric could replicate.

One customer had kept a pair of her father’s vintage jeans long after he had stopped wearing them. The jeans no longer suited his style, but she had preserved them anyway.

After discovering Re-Kriti, she sent the jeans three weeks before her birthday and asked the team to turn them into a bag. Along with them came a handwritten note thanking the team for allowing something that belonged to her father to become something she could now carry herself.

Stories like these, Bajracharya says, become “fuel” during periods when sales are poor and she questions why she started the business at all.

Re-Kriti has also tried to take upcycling outside its own production space.

Since 2025, it has organised five ‘Upcycling Mela’ events at colleges. Around 150 students and 20 teachers have participated, either bringing old jeans for Re-Kriti to transform or taking part in upcycling activities themselves.

That participation matters because Bajracharya believes Nepal does not necessarily suffer from a lack of conversations about sustainability.

If anything, she thinks there are too many.

Every Environment Day, every Plastic Free July and at sustainability programmes throughout the year, similar conversations return.

“We are only having conversations,” she says. “We are having too many conversations, honestly.”

What is missing, she argues, is action.

A person may hear repeatedly that overconsumption is harmful, but the idea becomes different when they hold an old pair of jeans, work with it and see it become something useful.

That is also why she believes changing consumer behaviour is more realistic than waiting for the fashion industry to transform itself. Consumers, however, make choices every time they purchase something.

Perhaps that is Re-Kriti’s larger experiment. Its work begins with jeans, but the question it poses is not whether an old pair can become a bag. It is whether people can learn to look at what they already own differently.

A pocket can become a wallet. A scrap can become a key ring. A father’s old jeans can become his daughter’s birthday bag. A skill learned by a home-based tailor can become a source of income.

And a pair of jeans someone was ready to throw away can still have somewhere to go. For Re-Kriti, sustainability begins there.

articles.title: New Kathmandu festival brings Tarkovsky, Kapadia and Nepali cinema together
articles.summary:
‘Licchavi Cinema Festival’ will hold its first edition in Kathmandu from 11 to 15 September 2026 at QFX Cinemas, Chhaya Centre, showcasing a curated programme of feature films from Asia and world cinema.

The festival grows out of Licchavi House’s commitment to cinema and cultural dialogue, as well as filmmaker Khyentse Norbu’s (Founder, Licchavi House) long-standing connection to Nepal.

The inaugural selection brings together films from Nepal, Bhutan, India, Pakistan, Thailand, France, Germany, Japan, and Russia. The programme places contemporary Asian cinema alongside major works from different periods and traditions, including films by Andrei Tarkovsky, Payal Kapadia, Khyentse Norbu, Deepak Rauniyar, Abinash Bikram Shah, and Tashi Gyeltshen.

The films include ‘The Cup’, ‘Elephants in the Fog’, ‘White Sun’, ‘The Red Phallus’, ‘All We Imagine as Light’, ‘Ghost School’, ‘Stalker’, ‘La Haine’, ‘Perfect Days’, and ‘Memoria’.

“What we are doing with this first edition is placing our own cinema in conversation with the world,” says Abishek Budhathoki, festival curator, Licchavi Cinema Festival. “Cinema literacy is not a specialist skill. It belongs to any audience willing to engage. We envision Licchavi Cinema to be part of that growth, and open to anyone who wants in.”

The festival takes the Garuda as its emblem to protect what is lasting in cinema, and to carry it toward audiences who might not otherwise encounter it. In Nepal, and across Buddhist and Hindu traditions, the Garuda is a protector and messenger, a figure that moves between realms and carries word from one to the other, belonging fully to neither sky nor earth.

The ‘Licchavi Cinema Festival’ will be held with the support of Kathmandu Metropolitan City and the European Union.

Licchavi Cinema Festival

When: 11 to 15 September

Where: QFX Cinemas, Chhaya Center, Thamel

Time: Will be released soon

Entry: Tickets will be available soon on Khalti

articles.title: Your skin needs a Nepal-specific routine for its climate, altitude and pollution
articles.summary:
There is much noise alongside some genuine information on the internet about how to take care of one’s skin. Information on the internet comes from people all over the world and may often not be applicable to Nepal. Given its climate, altitude, and specific problems such as urban pollution, people’s needs will differ and require tailored solutions.

Dr Shreya Bastakoti is a consultant dermatologist and cosmetic surgeon at Lavana Skin and Hair Clinic in Kathmandu, Nepal. She obtained her MD in dermatology from Kathmandu University and received aesthetic training in Bangkok and Mumbai.

Bastakoti, who provides aesthetic services to patients with diverse dermatological concerns, discusses common skincare problems in Nepal and how people can adapt their routines to the country’s varied climate, altitude, and seasons.

What are the issues that people living specifically in Nepal face in terms of skincare?

Skin concerns in Nepal vary significantly depending on geography, altitude, climate, and lifestyle.

In the mountainous regions, low temperatures, dry air, strong winds, and high UV exposure can lead to dry and sensitive skin, chapped lips, sunburn, pigmentation, premature ageing, and, in severe conditions, frostbite.

In urban areas such as Kathmandu, air pollution is an important concern. Prolonged exposure to pollutants can disrupt the skin barrier and contribute to dryness, irritation, acne, pigmentation, and premature skin ageing.

In the Tarai and warmer, humid regions, heat, sweating, and friction create favourable conditions for fungal infections, intertrigo, folliculitis, acne, and heat rashes.

How does the monsoon season affect these problems compared to the dry season?

The monsoon season, with its high humidity and increased environmental moisture, can significantly influence several skin conditions. The warm, humid climate creates an ideal environment for fungal growth, leading to an increase in fungal infections, pityriasis versicolor, and intertrigo.

Increased sweating and occlusion may also contribute to acne and folliculitis flare-ups. Additionally, people may experience more allergic reactions, including those triggered by pollen, insects, and environmental allergens.

In contrast, the dry season generally has lower humidity, resulting in fewer fungal and moisture-related skin problems, although dryness, irritation, and skin-barrier disruption may become more prominent. Overall, skincare needs to be adapted according to the seasonal climate.

What is the importance of sunscreen in the high altitudes and plains in Nepal?

Sunscreen is an essential part of skincare throughout Nepal, particularly because of the country’s significant variation in altitude and consistently high levels of ultraviolet (UV) exposure.

At high altitudes, UV radiation is stronger because the atmosphere provides less filtration, and exposure is further intensified by reflection from snow and other surfaces. This increases the risk of sunburn, pigmentation, premature skin ageing, and cumulative UV-induced skin damage. Therefore, regular use of a broad-spectrum, high-SPF sunscreen is particularly important for people living at or travelling to higher elevations.

In the plains and lower-altitude regions, although UV intensity may differ, prolonged exposure to strong sunlight remains an important concern. Sunscreen helps prevent tanning, pigmentation, photoaging, and long-term UV-related skin damage.

How can people take good care of their skin in these circumstances?

I always believe that good skincare is about keeping it simple and being consistent, rather than using many products. You do not necessarily need an elaborate 10-step routine to maintain healthy skin. The basics—a gentle face wash, a moisturiser suited to your skin type, and a broad-spectrum sunscreen—are often enough for most people.

The routine should also be adapted to the environment. In cold, dry or high-altitude areas, a richer moisturiser and regular lip balm can help protect the skin barrier. In hot and humid regions, lighter, non-comedogenic products may be more comfortable and help reduce excess oil and sweating. Sunscreen should be used daily, especially when there is significant sun exposure, and reapplied when outdoors for prolonged periods.

Most importantly, avoid constantly changing products or following every skincare trend. Healthy skin comes from the right products, used regularly and appropriately for your individual skin needs

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Hamilton
articles.summary:
Hillcrest functions as the primary campus neighbourhood for Hamilton, operating essentially as the city's main student hub. Rather than a quiet suburban zone, Hillcrest is highly energetic and packed with student flats, local takeaways, and young people walking to lectures. The neighbourhood is completely dominated by university culture, making it the central gathering point for the local international student community.

People can save time and money because they can walk to classes and the university library within minutes, completely eliminating daily bus or parking costs.

Housing demand is incredibly high at the start of semesters, meaning competition for good rooms is fierce, and properties can suffer from student-related noise.

Silverdale serves as a peaceful alternative to the busier streets of Hamilton. It functions as a relaxed retreat where students can study quietly but still reach campus in under five minutes.

Rents are reasonable, and the neighbourhood offers a much calmer, quieter environment that is perfect for focused study.

The area lacks its own major nightlife or dining scene, so people will have to travel to neighbouring suburbs for entertainment or grocery shopping.

Nawton is a well-established residential suburb located on the western side of Hamilton, far from the main university campus. It serves as an excellent hideaway for budget-conscious students who want to escape the university bubble completely.

Weekly rental prices here are among the lowest in the entire city, letting you get a much larger room or property for a lower price.

The commute to the university is long and requires catching a bus through the city centre.

Dinsdale sits elevated on the western hills of Hamilton, acting as a highly independent and fully self-contained suburban community. Rather than just a collection of houses, it features its own comprehensive shopping centres, supermarkets, and medical clinics that cater to all daily needs.

Access to the local amenities means people can buy cheap groceries and essentials right on their doorstep.

Distance from the eastern campus means people are completely dependent on public transport schedules or owning a car to get to their classes.

Hamilton East

Hamilton East is one of the city’s oldest and most character-filled suburbs, blending a trendy heritage vibe with student living. It serves as a creative bridge perfectly positioned right between the university campus and the central business district.

It offers the lifestyle balance in Hamilton, giving students immediate access to food, local employment opportunities, and vibrant weekend river walks.

The charming, older character homes can be poorly insulated, making them quite cold and expensive to heat during the damp winter months.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Hamilton.

articles.title: Two Nepalis killed on Romanian railway track
articles.summary:
